title: Case study: Kabwe, a mining town at risk

blocks.heading: The case study: a town on contaminated ground
blocks.text: A required case study of an area where economic development is taking place and causing the environment to be at risk: Kabwe, a mining town in central Zambia - the development, the risks left in soil and air, and the management now catching up.

blocks.heading: The town and its mine
blocks.text: Kabwe lies in central Zambia, about 140 kilometres north of the capital, Lusaka, on the main north-south railway; the settlement began as a mining camp and the town grew straight around the workings. Lead and zinc were mined and smelted there from about 1906 until the mine closed in 1994, and the works stood in the middle of the town they had created. Townships such as Kasanda and Chowa sit beside the old workings and waste dumps, and the town is still growing, with families building on flat land that includes the old dumps.

blocks.heading: How development put the environment at risk
blocks.text: The risk was built in two ways. First, the smelter: nearly ninety years of lead-rich smoke settled over the townships, so lead passed into the soil where children play. Second, the waste: the dumps left at the close of mining lie open to the wind, and in the dry season fine lead-bearing dust lifts off them onto streets, roofs and food. From the ground the lead reaches people: children swallow it with the soil and dust on their hands and meals, and lead is a poison that harms the developing brain and nervous system. Studies in the 2000s and 2010s found soil-lead values many times above guideline levels and some of the highest blood-lead levels recorded in children anywhere - the threat sits in the environment, but the harm lands in people.

blocks.heading: Managing the legacy
blocks.text: The response shows what management looks like when risk was left unchecked for decades. A clean-up backed with international funding, begun in the late 2010s, has been capping the worst dumps with clean soil and treating the ground around homes and schools, while health teams test children's blood. The work is slow because the pollution sits in the soil itself rather than in one pipe that can be closed - the sharpest lesson of the case: risks prevented while development is taking place cost far less than risks left to settle into the ground.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Kabwe ties this topic to its neighbours: mining as an economic activity (topic 3.3), development and its measurement (topic 3.1), and pollution (topic 3.6 for water).
